title: Ten years in, $1,967. And at forty?
hook: $1,000 at 7% a year. The first ten years earn $967. Guess the next thirty.

knows: that a savings account pays interest

misconception: Savings grow in a straight line: if ten years earns about $1,000, forty years earns about $4,000.
objective: The learner can explain that compounding pays interest on past interest, so each decade earns more than the one before, and that over long periods interest-on-interest becomes most of the balance.

claims.text: With interest compounded once a year, a balance after t years is deposit × (1 + rate)^t.
claims.source: Each year multiplies the balance by (1 + r). Standard result, e.g. Brealey, Myers & Allen, Principles of Corporate Finance, ch. 2 (future values).

claims.text: $1,000 at 7% a year grows to about $1,967 after 10 years (a gain of $967) and about $14,974 after 40 years.
Simple interest (7% of the original $1,000 each year, never on past interest) pays $2,800 of interest over 40 years, a balance of $3,800; the stage shows this as the 'Plain 7% only' readout.
Extending the first decade's $967 gain in a straight line would give about $4,900 after 40 years.
In year 31 to 40 the balance grows by about $7,362, roughly 7.6 times the $967 earned in years 1 to 10.
After 40 years at 7%, interest earned on past interest is about $11,174, roughly three quarters of the $14,974 balance.
At 7% a year, money roughly doubles every 10 years.
The lesson is a model: a fixed rate every year, yearly compounding, no withdrawals, fees, taxes or inflation. Real returns vary year to year.
claims.source: Assumptions of the lesson's own calculation in Demo.tsx.

claims.text: At 7% a year each decade adds about twice what the decade before added: $967, $1,903, $3,743 and $7,362 for years 1–10, 11–20, 21–30 and 31–40.
claims.source: 1000 × (1.07^(10d) − 1.07^(10d−10)) for d = 1..4: 967.15, 1,902.53, 3,742.57, 7,362.20; each ratio is 1.07^10 = 1.967. Shown on the v2 stage as the decade row and in the reveal. Added v2.

claims.text: The dashed line on the stage keeps the first decade's pace ($96.72 a year) forever; it reaches about $4,869 at 40 years, labelled on the stage as 'first-decade pace: $4,900'.
claims.source: 1000 + (967.15 / 10) × t; at t = 40: 4,868.6 (the reveal rounds it to $4,900, claim c8). Added v2.

recall.question: Savings grow at a fixed 7% a year. Which decade adds the most money?
options: All decades add about the same
recall.why: Each year's interest is paid on a bigger balance, including all the earlier interest, so later decades add more.
